reason: The court decided recoverable pro-rata costs in a partition action on the appraised value, so the statement is overbroad and drops the partition-law context.
The court held that a donee whose interest devolved under the deed of gift could be substituted under section 404 to continue the action.
The extracted statement and quote are truncated and omit the actual appeal-time computation rule and bond default holding.
The court denied a section 712 citation for post-death rents absent a due-administration need, not a general entitlement to rental income from an estate.
The court held that a minor's sale of immovable property with guardian assistance but without court sanction carried a presumption of invalidity.
The court construed 'Court' restrictively only in section 48(4)(a)'s partition-law context, not as a general definition for all uses.
This is a general interpretive canon used in the reasoning, not the case's operative holding on the partition survey return date.
Notice of the returnable date was part of the statutory context, but the usable holding was the computation of the 30 days from receipt in open court.
The court applied section 147 and held that disposal on a preliminary issue requires a pure question of law going to the root of the case.
The extraction changed the holding from no Rent Board application being required to 'without making an admission,' which the quote does not support.
The court held that a landlord owning no house or not more than one residential premises may maintain a reasonable-requirement ejectment action.
The court held the action was really under section 22(2)(bb), not section 22(2)(b), so the statement reverses the point.
The maxim was applied only to the wrong Rent Act paragraph where the parties were not misled, so the statement is too broad as a standalone rule.
The court held that a duly appointed Assistant Commissioner could exercise the Commissioner's powers within the appointed area.
The court held that the Prescription Ordinance regulates civil actions and does not apply to Agrarian Services Act proceedings.
The alleged estoppel would have been against the landlord, and the court rejected it because legally fixed rent left no duty to protest.
The court held that documents chargeable under section 2 remain exempt if they fall within section 5, including the leave-to-appeal affidavit before it.
The vicarious-liability rule was the holding, but the cited statute section is Civil Procedure Code section 40 rather than the provision construed for this rule.
The prescription-from-death holding is supported, but Civil Procedure Code section 40 was not the statute construed for that rule.
The court construed section 40 and held that pleading the facts, claims, and reliefs in the plaint was sufficient compliance.
Saying the amendment is relevant is not the court's legal holding and the quote supports a much narrower time-bar rule.
The statement captures that section 71(2)(aa) operated as a time bar but drops the crucial qualification that it did not affect pre-2 May 1984 pending applications.
The court held that a partition party liable for owelty or compensation cannot obtain delivery of possession until payment, with time running from payment.
The statement is too vague to state the actual holding about section 52(1), owelty or compensation, and the Civil Procedure Code time bar.
The quote records a fact-specific appellate misdirection, while the real holding concerned the parties' paper and prescriptive title rather than a standalone legal rule.
